Therefore I would say that if you are going to bring down the price of agricultural products you will first of all have to bring down the price of things that enter into their cost. As far as I know there is only one commodity in this country the price of which is controlled, and that is wheat. Is the price of wheat too high or too low? The price of wheat today is lower than it was in 1948 and 1949, the last two years of the British wheat agreement. At that time it was $2 a bushel. Today under the international wheat agreement it is $1.80 or $1.89

in Canadian funds. Since that time, however, the cost of living has risen 35 points. Therefore how can anyone say that the price of wheat is as high as it should be?
What is the basis of the price of wheat today? It is nothing more or less than government guessing or speculation. I say that for this reason. In 1948 and 1949, when we were discussing the international wheat agreement in this house, I criticized the agreement on the ground that in trying to set the price of wheat in advance the government were merely guessing as to what the price should be. Therefore I urged that, instead of guessing at a price for the future, they should tie the price of wheat to the price level so that if the price level went up the price of wheat would go up and if the price level went down the price of wheat would go down. That would be fair to both the consumer and the producer because if the price level went down the farmers should be able to buy things more cheaply and therefore could afford to take less for their wheat. If, on the other hand, the price level went up they should receive a higher price for their wheat because they would have to pay a higher price for the things they would have to buy. In other words, we have been consistently subsidizing the Canadian consumers, and at the present time the farmers are actually receiving 43 cents a bushel less for their wheat than is obtained by the wheat board for what they sell to nations outside the international wheat agreement as class II wheat.
I disagree entirely with the statement that was made by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. LaCroix) during his speech. He wanted an embargo placed upon the export of cattle. Why pick out beef alone? Why say there should be an embargo on the export of cattle? What about other commodities in short supply that are exported, thus causing higher prices? I would say that the farmers would very much like to see the government place an embargo on the export of lumber. For the past few years we have had a great deal of difficulty in getting the lumber we wanted in western Canada, and the price of lumber has risen to a far greater extent than the price of farm commodities. In the early stages of the war one could buy No. 1 shiplap in the west for $30 a thousand. Today for lumber that is far inferior in quality you have to pay $120, an increase of over 300 per cent. When people start talking about an embargo on any agricultural commodity let them at the same time ask for an embargo on the export of these things that enter into the cost of producing farm commodities.
The Address-Mr. Quelch
The main reason there is so much misunderstanding with respect to the price of agricultural products in Canada today is the fact that the bureau of statistics has been using the 1935-39 period as the basis for their price index. It is well to remember that during that period the prices of farm products were away below the cost of production. They were at the depression level. Farmers were having to allow their capital to depreciate. During that period they had to accept a standard of living far below what might be considered subnormal. Therefore with such misunderstanding regarding agriculture farmers are somewhat dubious about asking the government to impose an over-all system of price control. Let the government introduce a parity formula into the Agricultural Prices Support Act. That would do more to remove that doubt than anything else the government could do.
I was very much interested in the speech by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance. I am not going to have time to deal with it fully, but I should like to refer briefly to the statements he made that interested me. He told us there were plenty of goods in the country, that there was no shortage. I see he is in the house so perhaps I should quote what he said. At page 159 of Hansard for October 18 he said:
Many countries have grave shortages of consumer goods and a great abundance of purchasing power. In this country today there is no real shortage of consumer goods.
Then again he said we have an excess of purchasing power and sufficient consumer goods; therefore there is no real shortage of goods in Canada. If there are plenty of goods then it cannot be charged that people are bidding against each other in order to get goods that are not in short supply. The goods are there. What does it mean? It merely means that industry today says to itself that there is enough money in circulation to pay higher prices than are being paid for certain goods, and they are going to have some of that money. Therefore they will raise prices. It is nothing more or less than a straight case of profiteering.
I will give the government a very good example of that. When it was announced over the radio that the cost of living had risen to 190-4 it was stated that the main cause of the increase was a rise in the price of textiles. What is the situation regarding the textile industry in Canada today? The textile industry is in a slump. It is having difficulty selling its production. The reason I say that is because I had a letter from a man in Norway wanting to come to Canada to work in the knitting mills. He wanted to

The Address-Mr. Quelch know what the chances of employment were. I telephoned the immigration department and asked what chance he would have to get a job in Canada. They said he could obtain a job in practically any industry except the textile industry because it is in a slump and is having difficulty in selling its production. What possible excuse is there for the textile industry to raise prices when they cannot sell their existing goods? Can the minister say there are too many dollars chasing too few goods? They have goods there that they cannot sell.
It is nothing more or less than a straight case of profiteering. The textile industry's sales were reduced and they wanted to maintain their profits, so they raised the price of their goods to try to get the same return from the sale of a reduced quantity. I was also told that the situation would be remedied very soon because large defence orders were pending which would put the textile industry back into full production. That being the situation, surely the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance would agree that the most logical way of dealing with it-a situation which is nothing more or less than straight profiteering and not a question of too many dollars chasing too few goods- would be price control. The best method would be price control, not instead of increased taxation, not instead of borrowing, but in addition to them. I would say that at the very least we could certainly impose price control on the mark-up of the goods imported into this country. Such a move would have a beneficial influence upon the prices of goods produced in this country.
In the few minutes left I should like to refer to one other matter. I believe the government made a mistake in raising the interest on savings bonds. By doing that the government is bound to increase the debt charges against the country. It is all very well to boast that you are reducing the amount of the national debt, but if you are going to increase interest charges you are going to increase the debt charges against the people. No doubt the minister will argue that if the government had not increased the interest rates on bonds the people would not have been willing to buy those bonds. After all if, in order to maintain the economy on an even keel, it is necessary to reduce the amount of purchasing power in circulation, and the government decides to do so by borrowing the savings of the people, then if the people refuse to buy savings bonds the government would be fully justified, in my opinion, in bringing in a system of compulsory savings such as existed during the war. After all, a system of compulsory savings provides a far more effective control over the money in circulation than any system


of selling bonds, because when the people buy bonds today they can sell them tomorrow if they so desire. The government has no control over that money. We know quite well that under pressure many people have bought bonds, and within a few weeks have sold them again. On the other hand if a system of compulsory savings were used to withdraw the money from circulation, then the government could keep that money out of circulation until such time as the general situation warranted returning it.
In closing I would say it is quite evident that the government's anti-inflationary measures have not been effective in controlling prices in this country. There does not appear to be any immediate likelihood that government policy will have that effect. Therefore until such time as the government is in a position to control prices effectively in order to lessen the burden on the people, I would say they are under a definite obligation to take steps to increase the purchasing power of those people who are in the extremely low income bracket. The group of people that come to my mind before any other group are the recipients of war veterans allowances. How can we expect people to live on $40 a month or $70 for a married couple under today's conditions? I was quite disappointed when the government announced it had no intention of setting up a committee to deal with this question this session. It is the intention to set up a committee next year, but in the meantime these people have to manage somehow or other on that miserable allowance. I believe the government should reconsider that action, and either set up the committee this session or take immediate action to increase the war veterans allowance to $50 a month for a single person and $100 a month for a married couple.

speechtext:
Like those who have preceded me in this debate, Mr. Speaker, at the outset I should like to pay tribute to the mover (Mr. Cauchon) and seconder (Mr. Simmons) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I believe the practice that has been followed in this parliament for many years is really an excellent one, that either the mover or seconder gives his address in the French language. It is very fortunate also that the members who participate in this debate are from different sections of this country. I was impressed with the sincerity of the remarks of the hon. member for Beauharnois. I felt that he had the interests of his people very much at heart, but with that he had a broad vision of the good of Canada as a whole.
I know all members were impressed with the zeal and vigour of the remarks of the

hon. member for Yukon-Mackenzie River. I only wish that more information about that marvellous northland of ours could be given to the rest of Canada. I feel it is too bad that more Canadian citizens have not emulated the example of two of our governors general *vho have gone from one end of the Yukon ;o the other, and have visited many parts of :he Northwest Territories. I thank the hon. member for Yukon-Mackenzie River for the splendid picture he painted of that great section of Canada which he represents, and for his conception of how his section can fit in with and benefit the rest of this country. Having members of this type demonstrates the size and might of this great country of ours.
Much has been said in this debate, and quite rightly so, on the subject of inflation. Inflation respects no man's position. No matter what his station in life, he has to pay for inflation. If it were a phenomenon peculiar to this country I would say the government could do something about it, but inflation is something that has swept across the whole world. If we in Canada were to say we were going to stop this insidious inflation, I believe we could be likened to King Canute who once stood on the seashore of England and ordered the waves of the ocean to roll back. The very sound of the word "inflation" is insidious. I was particularly interested, and I might say educated, by the remarks of the member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair). I consider that in his speech he outlined, concisely and logically, the influences that have brought about inflation throughout the world, and the influences that are at work within our own country.
I have this morning's issue of a newspaper which has never been known to shout the virtues of the Liberal party from the housetops. I should like to quote from an editorial appearing in the Montreal Gazette, in which much of the debate that has taken place in this house on the subject of inflation is condensed. Mention is also made of the breakthrough of prices beyond the control limit set in the United States. Referring to the actions of this government the editorial states:
By declining to impose price controls now the government of Canada has not taken, politically speaking, the easiest course. But it has taken, economically speaking, the soundest one.
Yes, it is much easier for the government to listen to the popular clamour than to what would be the practical solution. Since the war certain other nations within the British commonwealth have consistently endeavoured to control prices. Probably the most outstanding example is Great Britain itself, where inflation has burst the bounds of any controls set by the socialist government
The Address-Mr. Fulford there. I know it is not pleasant to make comparisons. As has been so well said, comparisons are odious. Nevertheless, last fall while travelling in Australia and New Zealand I discovered that the chief hue and cry in those two sister countries in the commonwealth was with respect to the high cost of everything. Taking into consideration the depreciated value of the pound and changing it into Canadian dollars we found that prices in Australia and New Zealand were high. Just this morning an article appeared in the Toronto Globe and Mail stating that prices have gone completely out of bounds in Australia, that the government over there are in a desperate condition and a serious quandary.
Actually, with regard to inflation there is a strange paradox. During a period of rising prices we find that people are prosperous, are working and are able to purchase articles. But if deflation is brought on, or if an attempt is made to bring down prices, unemployment becomes rife, wages are lowered, and the purchasing power of the people is reduced, with all the consequent evils that follow. Much as we should like to see a great reduction in present prices, I do not believe it would be to the general good of Canada to have this condition brought about even if we could do so; and I have read what economists have said with regard to this matter. If we take the advice of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and control our purchasing, try to produce more-whether it be by longer hours or by improved machinery-and increase the amount of consumer goods in the country, a levelling off could be effected. If we could do that it would certainly be possible to maintain a price level, high as that may seem to be to many.
Certainly in times such as ours people would not tolerate rationing. Anyone who has been to England in recent years-that is, in years since the war-will have found that one of the chief topics of conversation everywhere in that country is condemnation of their rationing laws. Reference has been made in this house to the matter of rationing, and it has been suggested that we in this country have purse rationing. I deplore remarks like that. They savour too much of soap box oratory, the kind that pits class against class, making some people envious of others. I do not think that type of approach is helping the situation any, nor do I think it contributes in any way to a solution of the problems that face us.
In that regard I should like to quote from the magazine Time of October 29, 1951, a statement attributed to Arnold J. Toynbee,

The Address-Mr. Fulford the great historian of this century. These remarks were published in the New York Times magazine:
Can we guess what the outstanding feature of our twentieth century will appear to be in the perspective of three hundred years? . . . My own guess is that our age will be remembered chiefly neither for its horrifying crimes nor for its astonishing inventions but for its having been the first age since the dawn of civilization, some five or six thousand years back, in which people dared to think it practicable ... to make the ideal of welfare for all a practical objective instead of a mere Utopian dream.
It is strange how two sets of eyes can see the same object in an entirely different light. A number of years ago my wife and I were travelling in Russia with some people who had leftist sympathies, to say the least. We visited workmen's clubs, and we would compare notes when we got back to the hotel. I would see the cracks in the walls where the snow was seeping through. The others who were with us would see the fire in the grate and the easy chairs. Some people can see Canada today as a country in which there is much want. Some can use statistical figures to show that all is not well. But in going around to factories I see the parking lots filled with workers' cars; in going into the average home I see all the modern electrical labour-saving devices, electric refrigerators, radios, washing machines, electrically stoked furnaces. One can see these evidences of prosperity all over the country, both in cities and through the rural districts. I believe what I see with my eyes. I would much prefer to rely on what I see in that way than on figures, drawn up by some statistician, purporting to prove something but which in reality just jumble the mind. At the risk of repeating an old cliche, I would remind hon. members of the old saying that figures do not lie but liars can figure.
The group for whom I personally have a great deal of sympathy are the so-called white collar group whose salaries have not gone up as have salaries in other lines of endeavour. I refer to clerks in the stores, bookkeepers and those in similar types of employment. I also feel for the elderly people who will be greatly helped by the old age pension when it becomes universal after January 1, but who nevertheless are forced to live on the income from low yield investments-the so-called blue ribbon investments such as government bonds-and whose income has remained constant in spite of the heavy increase in the cost of living. I feel that a definite effort should be made to help persons in that class.
Actually it is rather amusing to me to see a certain section of the Canadian press condemning this government for having a surplus. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that if it were


a deficit rather than a surplus that same section of the press would be howling to the hilltops. I feel that, having regard to our financial affairs Canada is the envy of the world. All we have to do is to look around and see the great amount of investment capital that is flocking into this country. Even if a certain group of Canadians do not feel that we are on financially sound ground, the rest of the world appreciates what we have over here. Is it any crime to write $500 million off the national debt this year? After all, $500 million off the national debt means an annual saving in interest of $15 million. At that rate it would take more than 20 years to write off all the national debt, but in so doing we would be saving $300 million a year in interest charges, or enough to pay family allowances.
I should like to take this opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to congratulate our Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris), and I wish he were in his seat. His policies are now beginning to bear fruit. I understand that up to the end of September we had received the largest number of immigrants that had entered Canada in any year since the war. Canada needs a larger population. Looking at it from the purely mercenary point of view, every immigrant who comes to Canada means that our per capita debt is decreased; but far more important than that, every immigrant who comes to our shores increases the earning power of our country. Many more are needed to develop the potential resources of Canada.
Last week it was indeed an inspiring sight for us sitting in this house to look up at the diplomatic gallery and see the soldiers, sailors and airmen wearing the uniforms of all the united nations who are fighting for the freedom of mankind in Korea. I am just a little afraid that a certain group of Canadians are becoming a bit complacent. We can be proud of the achievements of our fighting men in Korea, yet at times one wonders whether they are not an almost forgotten lot. There is a type of person who feels that the Korean expeditionary force is useless. That is the type of person who must be aroused from his lethargy. One excellent way of arousing him from that lethargy is to have a properly organized civil defence service. I was very glad to read in this morning's Globe and Mail a statement by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) to the good roads conference held in Toronto last Saturday night, in which he outlined the progress that has been made in regard to the civil defence organization in this country. On the night of October 24 the town of Brockville had the honour of having the Minister of

National Health and Welfare as its guest. We also had many more people who are important in the public life of this country. Along with the minister came Major General F. F. Worthington, civil defence co-ordinator; Colonel M. P. Cawdron, General Worthington's assistant; Fire Marshal W. J. Scott of Ontario; Colonel K. B. F. Smith, representing Hon. G. Arthur Walsh, Ontario co-ordinator; R. Richter Townsend, chief of the New York state bureau of fire and personal representative of Governor Thomas E. Dewey. There were also representatives from the municipal councils of many neighbouring communities, mayors and aldermen from Cornwall, Prescott, Smiths Falls, Gananoque, Kingston, who had come to see the civil defence demonstration that was put on. I only regret that so little publicity was given this event, because it made me very proud of the town that I have the honour to call my home. It was a splendid exercise and was highly complimented by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, who stated that other communities right across Canada could well emulate the progress that had been made in Brockville in regard to civil defence.
At this point I would like to pay a special tribute to C.B.C. Broadbent, the co-ordinator for the town, who came to Ottawa last winter to attend the special civil defence school that was held here. I shall not go into the mechanics of the event except to say that 500 or 600 citizens took part. Each one was given a special duty. Theoretically the town had been raided by an enemy through the air. Each one know what his duty was, but no one knew where the targets were to be. A central control office was set up about three miles out, which was kept informed by wireless of the targets that were hit. The whole community co-operated. There was a virtual blackout from eight o'clock in the evening until ten o'clock. Very few disregarded the appeal of the mayor to see that all lights were out in the homes and in the shop windows, or if they were left on the blinds were firmly secured. There was the closest co-operation among such organizations as the medical profession, the nursing profession, the St. John Ambulance Corps, the Red Cross, the league of frontiersmen	and	all private	citizens.Special mention	should be	made	of theco-operation of	the	police	departments,
municipal, provincial and federal, as well as the Brockville fire department.
All who saw	this	event	were	greatly
impressed, especially the representative who had come from Albany, New York, as the representative of Governor Dewey. At this point I should like to mention that towns along the international border had offered
The Address-Mr. Fulford to send no fewer than 40 pieces of firefighting equipment. Right up to last moment it was thought that they would be able to do this. Unfortunately it was found that there are no statutes in Canada granting immunity against personal or property damage to vehicles participating in a civil defence demonstration. For the good of all communities which are to set up these demonstrations, action should be taken in this country to see that those taking part in the demonstration are not held liable for any damage that may be caused. I mention that also because of the fact that every panel truck in Brockville was commandeered as an emergency ambulance. Everyone who owned a panel truck got it out; yet each one of those men was taking a chance in participating in this event if there had been an accident.
To make the exercise more realistic an attempt was made to obtain aeroplanes at either Trenton or Uplands from the Royal Canadian Air Force. In spite of the earnest efforts of the town and others we were unable to get this co-operation. I suggest that closer co-operation could and should exist between the Department of National Defence and the co-ordinators of civil defence operations. I know the criticism has been made that insufficient funds have been voted for civil defence in Canada. Perhaps it would be interesting to the house to know that, with 500 or 600 people who participated in this event and put on this most realistic demonstration, the total cost to the community was less than $300. I would add that, so far as the equipment was concerned, that provided by the Department of National Health and Welfare and the province of Ontario was adequate, and will serve well in* the event that, some day, it may be necessary for civil defence forces to go into action. Certainly this demonstration drove home to the minds of the people of the community the fact that attack is not inevitable. Certainly it drove home to them the fact that we are living in perilous times. I can assure the house that any complacency that may have existed was dissipated after this magnificent display was put on.
No member from eastern Ontario could help mentioning in this debate the St. Lawrence seaway. I should like at the outset to pay special tribute to the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Laing) who took a broad and magnanimous view by stating that in building the seaway a large part of Canada would benefit materially, and that what was good for any part was good for the whole. I say it was a magnanimous view because there have been others who have not shared that view and who, I am afraid, have allowed

The Address-Mr. Fulford sectionalism to interfere with the breadth of their vision. We have seen this great scheme buffeted from pillar to post for many years in the legislative chambers of our neighbour to the south. I only wish it were possible for the American people to realize that what is good for Canada is good also for them; and that whereas we will benefit materially from the building of the St. Lawrence seaway and the development of its tremendous hydroelectric energy, they will benefit equally and perhaps to an even greater extent.
Recently-and I say "recently"; to be specific I have here the issue of June 9, 1951 -there appeared in the English magazine The Sphere a series of pictures. I wish it were possible to have them reproduced in Hansard. However, I shall read the short article accompanying the pictures because I believe it reveals the great awareness in Europe of the tremendous advantages of canal systems for both navigation and hydroelectric purposes. I believe it will be of interest to hon. members to see how this great Rhineland canal system has been financed. The article accompanying the picture is as follows:
One of the most remarkable changes which has taken place in Europe in modern times is the rapid growth of Swiss trade and industry. Zurich, where the 600th anniversary celebrations recently took place, is now one of the great commercial capitals of the continent, and Basle, second city of the confederation, is now one of the most important traffic centres of Europe, not least because of its loading and unloading facilities at its extension of the Rhine lateral canal, known as the Grand canal of Alsace, which is now being pushed northward from Kembs to Ottmarsheim. The sections involved in these latest extensions are in French territory, and from a hydro-electric point of view France will be a big beneficiary, notably from the new power station at Ottmarsheim; but the implications as far as Switzerland is concerned- are immense, for Basle more than ever looms as one of the great river ports of the Rhineland system. This linked with the fact that the large area of the Swiss midlands between the Alps and the Rhine has developed more and more as a manufacturing area, although still retaining the aspect of an agricultural province, means that exports and imports are likely to flow ever faster along this famed route.
Construction work began on the extension of the Grand canal of Alsace in April, 1948, the plan, financed by Marshall aid funds and equipment, involving the excavation of 19,000,000 cubic metres of banking, the construction of two locks and the building of one new power station at Ottmarsheim.
The most modern plant has been brought in mostly from America, and the scheme is so far advanced that the opening of the new section of the canal is forecast for November.
This is by no means the end of the scheme. Between Basle and Strasbourg there is a difference in level of 60 feet, and it is hoped eventually to extend the canal system all the way northwards to Strasbourg, France's great eastern port, building en route no fewer than five more power stations. The scheme will be a blessing to the whole Rhineland, bringing electrical power to farms and to industry and to a host of homes.
For the Swiss, who have remained so steadfastly outside the turmoil of modern Europe, these Marshall aid works have no charitable implications,

for Switzerland is well able to pay in dollars for all her imports from the U.S.A. and her special position in relation to E.C.A. is fully recognized.
Switzerland, however, has urgent problems to face with regard to industrial development and electrical generation.
In the former category she has two other big canal schemes in mind. One relates to the linking of the Rhine and the navigable Rh6ne by the Helvetia canal along her western border.
Looking at a map of Europe I learned that Basle is approximately 400 miles from the sea. So that hon. members may have some idea of the size of this canal, I shall read the description of one of the illustrations showing a lock now nearing completion, so they may compare it with the size of the locks at the American Soo and the locks on the Welland canal. It states:
One of the mighty locks on the Grand canal of Alsace; This lock on the new section north of Kembs is 600 feet long, 74 feet deep and 75 feet wide. It is hoped that this section, extending northwards from Basle towards Strasbourg, will be open in November.
I know nothing can be said in this chamber to influence the policies of another country. It does seem deplorable, however, that the country which is financing this tremendous scheme in Europe has not seen fit to help us develop the mighty St. Lawrence seaway. But if that unwillingness persists, then I am very glad to see that government policy in Canada has been stated to the effect that Canada will complete the St. Lawrence seaway by her own efforts. Such a development would bring cheaper freight rates to the farmers of western Canada, enable the development of the great Labrador ore fields, and make available vast quantities of electrical energy which, in Ontario alone, would amount to no less than 1,100,000 horsepower. It would make every lake port a potential seaport, and bring the trade of the world to the middle of this great continent.
As I have mentioned, there has been certain opposition to this scheme, though it is hard for me to understand why there should be. It seems to be purely of a sectional nature. Attempts have been made to make central Canada look as though it wanted no other part of Canada to be developed, but that is not the case. This is a matter that transcends all party lines. I am sure every hon. member wants to see the natural resources of Canada properly developed. If the west coast needs developing, if Alberta or any other section of the prairie provinces needs developing, if the maritimes are in need of development this parliament is ready to give earnest and sincere attention to all such matters brought before it.
We in Ontario are anxious to see the coal and steel industry of Nova Scotia prosper. We are interested in the possibilities of the

Passamaquoddy scheme. We would like to see Cape Breton connected to the mainland by a causeway. We would like to see the eventual construction of the Chignecto canal. These are not sectional matters; they are things that pertain to all of Canada. I think all hon. members want to see the great natural resources of this country developed for the future welfare of the people of our land.
Perhaps eastern Ontario will benefit most from the development of power, as there will be literally 1,100,000 horsepower at our back door; but eastern Ontario would not expect to have any power which it is not equipped to take. It is up to us to see that we do our share in developing the industries and natural resources of this section of the country so we will be able to take our share of the power. We do not want to see it all go to central Ontario, and I know it will not.
The first iron smelter in Upper Canada was opened in Leeds county, which I have the honour to represent, over one hundred years ago. The first lead mine in Upper Canada was operated there. I can remember in my own time when mica and graphite were mined to a large extent in the county. The ores are still there and perhaps with modern methods and cheap power it may again be profitable to work these veins. We have all watched with the greatest interest the development work of the Bethlehem steel corporation at Marmora, north of Belleville. I am not a geologist, but I am told that the same outcropping of rock extends all over this section of the province.
As I say, one hundred years ago iron ore was mined in Leeds county, put in barges and taken through the Rideau canal to Kingston, where it was transshipped to lake ports to be smelted. That traffic stopped with the discovery of the Mesabi range, but the Mesabi range may no longer be the great producer of ore it used to be. It may be that the great natural resources of eastern Ontario can again be economically developed.
We cannot conclude a discussion of the St. Lawrence seaway without remarking on the splendid co-operation that has existed between the premier of Ontario, the chairman of the hydro electric commission and the federal authorities. I regret that this matter has been brought into the provincial political field. A project that means so much to our country should never be brought down to the level of petty politics. I am sure the vast majority of the people of Canada realize that it is only through the co-operation of the provincial and federal governments that such a scheme can be brought into successful operation.
The Address-Mr. Gagnon
The St. Lawrence seaway has been the dream of all of us who live in the eastern part of this province. As a little boy I remember men discussing the possibilities of the seaway. We actually believe it will be started with or without the co-operation of the United States. We cannot help but feel confident that the great natural resources of this country will be usefully and economically developed by means of this great power development which will serve the whole Dominion of Canada. Beneficial results will be felt in all sections of the country, in the prairie provinces and in Labrador, that great new part of our tenth province. Again I repeat that what is good for any part of Canada is good for the whole.

Mr. Speaker, the speech on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, in addition to providing me with an opportunity of congratulating the mover and seconder, also allows me to say a word or two on a subject I had already broached during the last session.
On June 27 of this year I drew the attention of the house to the case of Flight Lieutenant J. J. Desrochers of Quebec, unfairly discharged from the R.C.A.F. after thirteen years of loyal and continued service.
The facts then reported were neither denied nor contradicted. The particulars stated were clear and true, and yet the questions put have remained unanswered.
When I stated that Flight Lieutenant J. J. Desrochers had been discharged because of justified activities in favour of French-speaking compatriots, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) answered that this man was discharged because he had failed to pass the qualifying exams in 1948, 1949 and 1950.
To set the record straight, to dispel all doubts in the minds of those who like to know how our fellow countrymen are faring and, above all, in justice to this young man, whose career was shattered by the French-baiting brass hats of the air force, I will read a letter written by Flight Lieutenant Desrochers, on July 2 last, to the newspaper Le Devoir, a copy of which he sent to me:
Quebec, July 2, 1951
Editor,
Le Devoir,
Montreal.
Sir,
With reference to your article of June 28. under the title "Mr. Gagnon tells the house about R.C.A.F. Officer J. J. Desrochers," I beg you to offer me the hospitality of your columns in order that I may enlighten the public with respect to the explanation the Hon. Brooke Claxton gave of my dismissal, In reply to the speech made by the independent member for Chicoutimi, Mr. Paul Edmond Gagnon.

The Address-Mr. Gagnon
The general staff which has undoubtedly forwarded to the Minister of National Defence the explanation that my dismissal had been necessary due to my having failed the 1948, 1949 and 1950 examinations, has misinformed the minister. I prove right now this statement by certifying that this same general staff which established these tests in 1948 stated in its official directions, R.C.A.F. Administration, Series F, that these tests were not compulsory and that their only purpose was to determine whether an officer was qualified for promotion from his present rank to the next higher rank in the military hierarchy.
I shall go further yet. I am submitting to this end an official document signed by Group Captain J. G. Stephenson, for the Chief of the Air Staff, under date of March 22, 1950, giving details as to the result of examinations I wrote in 1950, from which it will be realized that I am asked to rewrite at the 1951 term the only subject in which I failed to secure the required marks: Current events.
If we admit the explanation of my dismissal as given by the minister, we are forced to the conclusion that the general staff had reversed its official decision signed on the enclosed document, to allow me to rewrite my examination during the following term and thus has given to the rules governing such examinations a unique interpretation in my case, namely to dismiss me, which, on the face of it, would be a gross injustice.
I wish to thank Le Devoir for its sympathetic view.
Yours very truly,
J. J. Desrochers,
42 St. Jean Baptiste, Beauport East, P.Q.
As is evident from this letter and the attached document, there is a contradiction between the statements of the Minister of National Defence and those of the person involved, Mr. Desrochers. As I do not doubt the latter's word, I am inclined to think the minister has been misled.
A full and impartial inquiry would shed light on that most unfortunate case, and I again request it from the minister.
If the government refuses to do so, and does not care to find and punish the guilty parties, it will be accused of collusion. I would then say that the government is conniving with those bent on destroying national unity, on persecuting Canadians of French descent and on putting my compatriots through a kind of military life that they find unacceptable.
Canada cannot efficiently defend itself without the help of the French element; yet it is humiliating to find how our compatriots are treated in the various services. We must relentlessly insist on our rights so that the bilingual character of our country be recognized, in the armed forces as elsewhere. The constitution that governs us should be respected without our having to protest and complain.
The brigade that will presently serve in Europe will comprise, if I am not mistaken, three infantry battalions and one artillery regiment.
I would like to know the names of the commanding officers of each of these battalions and also whether the orders given to the French-Canadian units will be given in French. I would also like to be assured that the soldiers from my province will not have to submit to the risks and inconvenience of particular affection such as is now the case in Korea where French Canadians are chosen for the most exposed positions in the line and the most unpleasant fatigues.
And will our troops, at last, have a typically Canadian flag, a symbol of a free and sovereign country?
Has the time not yet come to bow to the wishes of those citizens whose one and only country is Canada and to give our country a distinctive ensign, free from all traces of colonialism? I most eagerly hope so as I most eagerly hope and wish for "O Canada" to be officially proclaimed our national anthem.
Mr. Speaker, the other remarks I wish to make today concern the government's foreign policy.
I have often urged in this house that our country send a representative to the Vatican and I have often deplored the fact that Canada remains one of the few nations officially without direct contact with the Holy See.
Newspapers representing all shades of opinion, political and religious, have on various occasions supported this view and all those who are abreast of international affairs or who are concerned about the struggle against communism realize the necessity of such diplomatic representation.
To the reasons already voiced in my previous speeches, I wish to add the unequivocal testimony of the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sinclair) and I wish to place on Hansard what he wrote on this subject last year. I am quoting from The Ensign:
(Text):
Canada is losing information by not having a diplomatic representative at the Vatican, says James Sinclair, parliamentary assistant to finance minister Abbott, and Liberal member of parliament for Coast-Capilano, B.C. Mr. Sinclair expressed his views in a letter of support to a Catholic women's league subdivision in Vancouver and to various Protestant groups who opposed the appointment. Following is the text of Mr. Sinclair's letter:
"During the ten years that I have been a member of parliament the matter of establishing diplomatic relations with the Vatican has been raised in parliament by private members. It has always been

raised by a Catholic member, and generally opposed by Protestant members; and so had the appearance of being a religious dispute. X had never given the matter much thought, but simply sided with the Protestants on this matter. However, for eight weeks this year I was in Europe settling post-war debts with eight countries, and so had the opportunity to see for myself the work being done by our diplomatic missions, and therefore to realize the importance of that work. Before the last war, Canada maintained missions in the United Kingdom, France, the United States and Japan. As a consequence of the very full part we played in winning the war, we found it necessary to expand the number of these missions, and today we maintain them in the hope that by reaching international understanding between our country and these other countries we may be able to prevent the misunderstandings which lead to international disputes and war. These missions serve two important purposes-to spread correct information about our country and our country's policies, and to gather and transmit the political views and economic problems of these countries to our own government at Ottawa. The gathering of this information is especially important today because of the cold war between the east and the west. It is for this reason we have missions today in Russia, Czechoslovakia, Poland and Yugoslavia, not as an indication that we approve of the government of those countries, but rather because we want to know as much about them and their future policies as possible. With communism fighting a world wide battle against the western world it is especially important for us to have all possible information about the activities of the communist countries and the communist movement.
The Catholic church is fighting communism wherever it exists, and it has no hesitation in accrediting representatives to even the communist governments, so that they may have all possible information. I met the Vatican's representative in Yugoslavia, and learned more from him about the country than I did from any other diplomatic representative in Belgrade.
This, and other experiences, have led me to the belief that Canada is losing information by not having a diplomatic representative at the Vatican, Almost every European nation, Protestant and Catholic, has such representation.
In Canada, where we are comparatively new to the necessity for diplomatic representation, the problem has been discussed almost entirely on religious grounds, and if an appointment were made at this present time, a large proportion of our people would regard it as a religious appointment, and so be strongly opposed to it. Public discussion of this situation, however, will bring about a better understanding, which might eventually lead us to have a representative in the Vatican, as does Protestant England. The most certain way then to assure the people of Canada that our representative was there for diplomatic reasons would be to have such Canadian ministers chosen from non-Catholic faiths.
(Translation):
Following this statement, it is interesting to read what is reported in The Ensign.
(Text):
It is now clear beyond argument that opposition to sending a representative from Canada to the Vatican is based on religious prejudice rather than on factual examination.
Canada is to continue on a colonial status of dependence on London and is to forego advantages of diplomatic exchange with the Vatican, now so widely accepted because the Pope is hot only
The Address-Mr. Gagnon
sovereign ruler of the independent state of Vatican City but is also Supreme Pontiff of the Catholic Church.
The beclouding of a political issue through the injection of religious prejudice naturally arouses more than mere interest amongst those against whom the prejudice is directed.
There is one special remark in Sinclair's statement which must be noted and acted upon. He implies that there is still great ignorance abroad about the Vatican and its role. Do we as citizens not owe it to our less informed citizens, even those now sitting in parliament, to destroy any vestige of ignorance on a subject with which we should be fully familiar?
Times are too serious and the needs of the hour too great to permit us to neglect any advantages we see for our country and the cause of freedom, justice and, above all, true understanding of what we ail, all who believe in God, face from our common godless enemy.
(Translation):
I am sorry to say that Canada was not represented when, in 1950, standing before 37 representatives of great and small nations who had met in his palace to hear an appeal for peace in international relations, the Pope scornfully referred to the attacks launched against the Vatican, adding that while the independent state in his keeping was bereft of military power, its peace potential was incalculable.
I hope that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), who was noncommittal when replying to a question I asked him recently about this matter, will soon take a decision and that, in accordance with an old custom of his predecessors, he will follow the example of civilized nations which deem it important to have an ambassador at the Vatican.
